title: Rapid Onramp ChatStream Console Demo
summary: AE + SE walked TideWave through a hosted-API onramp: live chat streaming, parameter trade-offs, retry/backoff patterns, and a brief tour of the Console Optimize recommendations. Customer is evaluating for a real-time chat assistant and cares most about low latency, predictable cost, and audit logs. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot and a performance benchmark on their typical 60-token messages at 100 req/min.

Parameter tuning: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
Retries, idempotency keys and exponential backoff
Console: Optimize suggestions, per-route cost/time breakdowns

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-07
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morales (Redwood AE), Sam Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (TideWave CTO), Priya Ramesh (Lead Eng), Ethan Cole (Product)
---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex from Redwood Inference, with me is sam our solutions eng. um quick agenda — live demo of the hosted chat stream, talk through params and retries, and then console optimize tour.
[00:18] Jordan: sounds good, we have about an hour. quick background — we run chat assistants in our app, goal is sub 200ms tail latency for short replies, and keep cost predictable.
[00:29] Sam: got it. when you say 200ms, is that end-to-end from client to first token?
[00:34] Jordan: yeah, from user click to first token displayed. most messages are 20-80 tokens.
[00:40] Alex: perfect. we'll show streaming which is how we return first token fast, and then some batching and cache tips to keep cost down.
[00:48] Priya: also, security: we need audit logs and SSO.
[00:51] Alex: yep — we covered SSO + audit in the onboarding doc, and we have KMS integrations for private deployments. we'll attach the security brief.
[01:03] Sam: jumping into demo — i'm in the console now. creating a chat sandbox, connecting to the hosted endpoint. note: the streaming toggle is on. i'm going to send a short prompt, you should see partial chunks appear.
[01:22] [demo noise - screen share clicking]
[01:28] Ethan: i'm seeing tokens come through incrementally — nice. latency to first token is about 140ms in this region.
[01:35] Sam: that is under typical conditions; tail spikes can happen with long KV caches or cold model variants. we recommend pinning a model variant for production if you need strict SLOs.
[01:46] Jordan: can you explain model variants? we don't wanna manage dozens.
[01:50] Alex: variants are compatible builds — e.g., quantized v1 vs fp16 v2 — same API surface, different perf/cost. smart routing will fallback to a compatible variant if the primary is overloaded.
[02:05] Priya: how does retrying factor in? if client sees an error, what should we do?
[02:10] Sam: three patterns — simple retry with exponential backoff, idempotency keys to prevent double-cost on retries, and optimistic streaming reconnection patterns for partial responses. here's pseudocode i just pasted into chat: use an idempotency key header, on 5xx do backoff 100ms -> 300ms -> 900ms, up to 3 attempts.
[02:34] Jordan: and about partial streams — if a stream cuts after a user sees partial text, do you re-request the rest or continue?
[02:41] Sam: we recommend using the last token offset as part of the idempotency metadata, or more simply re-request with the prior prefix as context so model knows to continue, but that increases token cost. prefix/KV caching can reduce that.
[02:58] Ethan: sounds like cost tradeoff. do you have console metrics that show tokens per session?
[03:03] Sam: yes — per-route token breakdown and a token-per-session median. also Optimize will suggest lowering temperature or truncating max_tokens if it sees waste.
[03:12] Priya: show Optimize?
[03:15] [demo - console navigation sounds]
[03:20] Sam: here is the Optimize tab — it surfaced a recommendation to shave 2 tokens from the max by using a stop sequence, and enable prefix caching for repeated starters. it's a lightweight suggestion, you can apply it to a route.
[03:34] Jordan: great. curious about concurrency — if we have 100 RPS, what's the best setup?
[03:39] Alex: for hosted, we'd recommend continuous batching with small per-request timeouts. the runtime automatically batches like 5-20 requests depending on seq length. for 100 RPS of short sequences, you'll likely keep single-digit GPUs in Dedicated, but hosted auto-scales.
[03:56] Jordan: mention of dedicated — we prefer hosted first but might move to dedicated if costs get high.
[04:02] Alex: totally normal. many customers start hosted for velocity, then move to Dedicated or Private once they hit predictable throughput.
[04:12] Priya: about logs and retention — can we keep audit logs in our S3?
[04:16] Sam: yes, logs can be exported, and we have per-request tracing hooks. encryption at rest via KMS.
[04:24] Ethan: any limitations on streaming with structured output or tool calls? we use function calls for some flows.
[04:30] Sam: streaming works with structured outputs, though some callbacks may require a finalization step; tool calling is supported but you might want to buffer tool invocation until final token is seen to avoid partial tool triggers — small nuance.
[04:46] Jordan: can we see a quick example of tuning temperature/top_p for deterministic responses?
[04:50] Sam: sure — lowering temperature to 0.0-0.2 and top_p to 0.8 gives more deterministic outputs. console lets you pin those as route defaults.
[04:58] Priya: is top_p applied after temperature? we had confusion from another vendor.
[05:02] Sam: order doesn't really matter in practice — both modify sampling distribution; the SDK documents interactions.
[05:10] [10m mark - slightly fuzzy audio]
[10:12] Jordan: back to retries — what HTTP codes mean immediate retry vs no-retry?
[10:17] Sam: retry on 5xx and 429 (with rate limit backoff), do not retry on 4xx client errors. some 500s are fatal but most are transient. we include Retry-After headers when applicable.
[10:30] Alex: also use idempotency-key header to dedupe. SE will provide a code snippet.
[10:36] Priya: ok. one more: do you support partial response caching for repeated prompts? our app often has same prefix question.
[10:44] Sam: yes — prefix/KV caching is supported in the runtime; the console Optimize will flag high overlap and recommend enabling prefix caching per-route. that can save up to 40% on tokens for repeated starts.
[11:00] Ethan: cool. about observability — can we correlate per-token cost to traces?
[11:05] Sam: yes, per-request breakdown is available at token granularity in the console and via the API. you can export traces to your telemetry backend.
[11:12] Jordan: security quick Q — do you keep customer data for training?
[11:16] Alex: we do not use customer data to train open models by default; we can provide contract language; Private deployments give you full control.
[11:25] [screen change - demo continues]
[20:03] Sam: switching to simulated high load — i'm firing 120 req/min for 60-token messages. notice the console latency chart — small tail spikes but healthy overall.
[20:18] Priya: what are the SLOs we can expect?
[20:22] Alex: for hosted we have SLOs per tier; we'll share the SLA doc. Dedicated offers tighter latency bounds.
[20:30] Jordan: what's the expected drop-in effort for our frontend real-time client?
[20:35] Sam: minimal — websocket or stream-over-HTTP patterns are supported; we provide SDK examples. the biggest change is handling partials and reconnections.
[20:45] Ethan: regarding cost, can Optimize provide unit cost estimates per route?
[20:48] Sam: yes — cost per token is surfaced and you can simulate cost under different param presets. Optimize will suggest quantization and route-level batch sizing.
[21:00] Jordan: can you recap pilot scope?
[21:04] Alex: 2-week hosted pilot, Redwood will provision sandbox routes matching your traffic pattern, run a benchmark at 100 req/min 60 tokens each, collect latency and cost metrics, and then we review results.
[21:16] Priya: confirm we can rotate keys and integrate with our KMS during pilot?
[21:20] Sam: yes, we support key rotation and customer-managed keys in Private; for hosted we have KMS-backed encryption and key controls we can detail.
[21:30] Jordan: ok good. next steps?
[21:33] Alex: i'll send pricing, pilot contract, security brief; sam will drop the retry pseudocode and param presets; you (Priya) will share traffic samples.
[21:44] Priya: will do.
[21:46] Ethan: Anything else — competitors? we evaluated Anthropic, OpenAI — why Redwood again?
[21:51] Alex: main reasons: production-first runtime with smart routing and caching, unified ops across hosted/dedicated/private, and clear Optimize tooling for cost/perf.
[22:05] [closing]
[22:07] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up by Friday.
[22:10] Jordan: thanks, bye.
---
